items.title: When we train an AI
items.subtitle: When we train an AI, we often ask for something like this: be as helpful as you can, but keep harm below a certain line.

items.title: "Do your best" and "never cross
items.subtitle: "Do your best" and "never cross this line" are different requests. How does a model follow both?

items.title: Over two hundred years ago
items.subtitle: Over two hundred years ago, the mathematician Lagrange came up with a way. It's called the Lagrange multiplier.

items.title: Making one thing as good as possible
items.subtitle: Making one thing as good as possible without crossing a line is called constrained optimization.

items.title: Lagrange's idea: don't build a wall.
items.subtitle: Lagrange's idea: don't build a wall. Put a price on crossing it.

items.title: Go a little over
items.subtitle: Go a little over, and you lose a few points. That price is the Lagrange multiplier, usually written λ.

items.title: Say a parent allows one
items.subtitle: Say a parent allows one hour of video games a day, and the kid keeps sneaking in more.

items.title: So the parent tries a new deal:
items.subtitle: So the parent tries a new deal: every extra minute costs a dollar of allowance, and every minute under earns one.

items.title: Set the price too low
items.subtitle: Set the price too low, and the kid goes over anyway. Too high, and he stops playing altogether.

items.title: Get it just right
items.subtitle: Get it just right, and he stops around the one-hour mark on his own. That just-right price is λ.

items.title: Let's try a small experiment.
items.subtitle: Let's try a small experiment. Here's a map of a mountain. Each ring is a contour line, the same height all the way round.

items.title: Our job is to find the highest spot.
items.subtitle: Our job is to find the highest spot.

items.title: But there's a rule:
items.subtitle: But there's a rule: stay inside the fence around camp. And the summit is outside it.

items.title: So we do it Lagrange's way:
items.subtitle: So we do it Lagrange's way: take the fence down, and charge λ points for every step away from the center of camp.

items.title: Then find the spot with the most height
items.subtitle: Then find the spot with the most height left after the charge. This dot marks it.

items.title: Start with a price of 0. No charge
items.subtitle: Start with a price of 0. No charge, so the dot runs straight to the summit, right out past the fence.

items.title: So we raise the price
items.subtitle: So we raise the price, and the farther outside the dot is, the more we raise it.

items.title: At a price of 1.5, the dot backs up a bit
items.subtitle: At a price of 1.5, the dot backs up a bit, but it's still outside. Raise it again, it backs up again.

items.title: At 3, the dot stops right on the fence.
items.subtitle: At 3, the dot stops right on the fence.

items.title: That's exactly the highest
items.subtitle: That's exactly the highest you can reach with the fence up: a height of 7.75.

items.title: Push the price to 4
items.subtitle: Push the price to 4, and the dot pulls back inside the fence, giving up height for nothing.

items.title: Now look at that just-right point.
items.subtitle: Now look at that just-right point. The contour line through it just touches the fence, so walking along the fence only takes you downhill.

items.title: That's the Lagrange condition:
items.subtitle: That's the Lagrange condition: at the best spot, the steepest way uphill goes straight out through the fence.

items.title: You might think λ
items.subtitle: You might think λ is just a knob we turned. But it also tells you how expensive the rule is.

items.title: Make the fence a tiny bit bigger
items.subtitle: Make the fence a tiny bit bigger, from a radius of 1.5 to 1.6.

items.title: The highest you can reach
items.subtitle: The highest you can reach goes from 7.75 to 8.04. That's a gain of about three times the extra radius.

items.title: So a λ of three means:
items.subtitle: So a λ of three means: loosen the fence a little, and you climb about three times that much.

items.title: Economists call this a shadow price.
items.subtitle: Economists call this a shadow price.

items.title: And if the summit
items.subtitle: And if the summit were already inside the fence, λ would be zero, because the rule wouldn't be holding you back.

items.title: So λ tells you which rules
items.subtitle: So λ tells you which rules are really pinning you down.

items.title: Back to where we started. In 2023
items.subtitle: Back to where we started. In 2023, a team at Peking University proposed a way to train language models. They called it Safe RLHF.

items.title: One scoring model rates
items.subtitle: One scoring model rates how helpful an answer is, another how harmful.

items.title: We want harm to stay under the line
items.subtitle: We want harm to stay under the line, and as much help as we can get.

items.title: They used a Lagrange multiplier:
items.subtitle: They used a Lagrange multiplier: take the helpfulness score, and subtract λ times the harm score.

items.title: And λ adjusts itself during training.
items.subtitle: And λ adjusts itself during training. When harm goes over the line, λ goes up, and safety counts for more.

items.title: When harm stays under, λ comes back down
items.subtitle: When harm stays under, λ comes back down, and the model is free to help more. Just like the dot on our mountain.

items.title: Prices on rules show up all over AI.
items.subtitle: Prices on rules show up all over AI.

items.title: Take regularization. It puts a price on complexity
items.subtitle: Take regularization. It puts a price on complexity, so the model doesn't just memorize the examples it's trained on.

items.title: And chatbots often pay a price for drifting
items.subtitle: And chatbots often pay a price for drifting too far from their original model.

items.title: So, to sum it up:
items.subtitle: So, to sum it up: a Lagrange multiplier is a price on a constraint.

items.title: Get the price just right
items.subtitle: Get the price just right, and you don't need a wall. You'll stop right at the line.

items.title: Next time you want it all
items.subtitle: Next time you want it all, but there's a line you can't cross, ask yourself: what is that line really costing me?
